source_refs.note: Topic 5.5.1.5 Boxplots (PDF 148, printed 145). Figure 5.8 is described in the text; the original diagram uses the chapter's Class A and Class B scores.

blocks.text: Boxplots, or box-and-whisker plots, summarize a distribution by showing the median, the quartiles and possible outliers, giving a visual summary of variability. They are useful for comparing groups, such as the exam scores of different classes.

blocks.alt: Six panels: a grouped bar chart of Class A and Class B scores, a line graph of daily earnings rising from 500 to 1,300 rupees, a histogram of ten exam scores in bins 50s to 90s with counts 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, a scatterplot of hours studied against marks with a dashed best-fit line, boxplots of Class A and Class B, and spreadsheet steps for making a chart.
blocks.caption: Five chart types using this chapter's data (original diagram after topics 5.5 and 5.6).
blocks.long_description: Bars compare categories, here each student's score in two classes. A line graph shows a trend over time, the earnings growing each day. A histogram shows a distribution: most of the ten scores fall in the 80s. A scatterplot shows a relationship: marks rise with hours studied, close to the line marks = 14.3 + 6.14 x hours. Boxplots compare groups: both classes have median 55, but Class B's box and whiskers are much wider. In Excel or Google Sheets you enter the data, select it, insert a chart, label it and then read what it shows.
